title: Tech giants race to get AI gadgets on shelves for holiday rush
content: With the holidays just months away, tech companies are betting this is finally the year that AI starts showing up under the Christmas tree. Apple , Amazon and Microsoft have all announced new devices in the past week with the aim of bringing generative artificial intelligence firmly into the home. Nearly four years after the launch of ChatGPT, the leading consumer tech companies are touting improved personal assistants and speedier on-device chips with AI capabilities as they try to sell new laptops, tablets, phones and smart home computers. Success is far from guaranteed. In addition to the weakest consumer sentiment data in 12 years due largely to stubborn inflation, and growing fears about the potential safety risks of AI, there's a learning curve that comes with the new technology. Jitesh Ubrani, an analyst at IDC, said tech companies want to introduce AI to consumers to lay the groundwork for more aggressive device launches in the coming years. "This is really about getting devices into consumers' hands, into consumers' homes, slowly teaching them how to use it, and getting feedback from them," Ubrani said, adding that new gadgets from Apple, Amazon and Microsoft aren't expected to sell in large volumes, at least not yet. Getting affluent early adopters on board now could be considered a win given the macro headwinds. Hardware prices across the board have risen, driven by soaring costs for components, especially memory and storage, as power-hungry AI servers suck up most of the capacity. Those price hikes have led to plunging shipments this year of new smartphones and laptops. Microsoft kicked off the launches last week by showing off an Nvidia -powered Windows laptop starting at $2,599, based around an AI chip called RTX Spark that can run powerful AI without relying on the cloud. Amazon followed by releasing Alexa tablets , the company's first pieces of hardware named after its smart assistant. The largest Alexa Tablet 12 Pro costs $550, compared to $155 for its predecessor, the Fire HD10. And on Tuesday of this week, Apple unveiled its HomeView smart home hub, powered by Siri AI. The $299 devices include a 7-inch screen that can be mounted, along with facial recognition software so it can be personalized for multiple family members. Analysts applauded Apple for introducing HomeView at a reasonable price given all the component shortages. "Apple has prioritized ecosystem adoption over immediate high hardware margins, delivering a local-AI hub at a price point that undercuts what a spec-heavy machine should logically cost," said Mohit Agrawal, who specializes in AI at CounterPoint Research, in an email. Dipanjan Chatterjee, an analyst at Forrester, said the shopping season will mark an early test of consumer demand for a new class of gadgets. "I think consumers are interested in what AI can do," said Chatterjee. "What's less clear is whether they are interested in buying hardware specifically because it is an AI device." Despite the many economic headwinds, the spending outlook heading into the holidays remains robust. Nearly half of U.S. consumers expect to spend the same or more this year compared to last year's holiday season, according to a McKinsey survey published in August. And Bain published a report last month, predicting that U.S. retail sales over the holidays will set new records and top $1 trillion for the first time. However, analysts cautioned "more than half of the nominal sales growth will come from higher inflation" pushing up prices. The firm predicted that sales in some electronics and appliances will remain flat. "In a time when folks are being a little money conscious, you say, 'Do I really need the next one of those, or could I drag out the replacement cycle on whatever it is?'" said Aaron Cheris, head of Bain's global retail practice, in an interview. "We've seen things that are discretionary purchases drag out longer." All three producers of the new AI gadgets emphasized their increasingly intelligent assistants, as well as more powerful chips to run them. Amazon said it's ditching the budget-friendly Fire family of devices in favor of three new Alexa Tablets that feature a more premium design with its souped-up AI assistant front and center. Users can say "Alexa" or tap the "Ask Alexa" button to summon the assistant and ask questions, get personalized recommendations or control their smart home. Amazon also introduced a hands-free mode, called "On-Screen Intelligence," that enables Alexa to read content on the tablet's display and take action, like preparing a shopping list based on a cooking video. Microsoft's new laptops with Nvidia chips can run AI coding models. Apple's HomeView uses Apple Intelligence to proactively show users their text messages, calendar appointments and photos. Apple expects users to talk to the device, and highlights Siri's ability to answer a broad range of questions, similar to the experience they have with modern chatbots. Apple also noted that HomeView uses the A18 chip, which was the fastest smartphone chip in the world when it was first introduced in September 2024. Carolina Milanesi, an analyst at researcher Creative Strategies, said companies will have to see if users are lured by the prospect of paying more for enhanced processing power. "Consumers out there are, I think, yet to be convinced that on-device matters as much, especially when you ask them to spend more for a device," Milanesi said. Ollama CEO Jeff Morgan said there's an audience for computers that give users control. His startup's open-source software allows people to install and use models on a variety of computers. "I think there's something about owning your AI versus renting it," he said. Then there's the longer-term opportunity that companies are pursuing, which involves getting consumers to buy subscriptions so they can lock in recurring revenue. Amazon's new Alexa requires a $19.99 monthly subscription, or Prime membership. Apple users have to buy an upgraded iCloud subscription to record secure video. Apple's biggest AI launch may come next week, when the company's new $1,999 iPhone Duo hits stores. The folding iPhone can display two apps side by side, including chats with Siri, offering a desktop-like interface for AI agents. WATCH: Amazon's Alexa tablets

title: ASML says it's getting order interest through 2030 as profit smashes expectations
content: ASML said Wednesday that some of its customers are expressing interest in placing orders for its critical semiconductor tools for 2029 and 2030 as the company reported third-quarter profit that beat expectations. The comments will likely comfort investors who have been looking to assess the longer-term demand outlook for ASML's lithography machines. "Our customers continue to increase their short- and medium-term equipment demand forecasts with us, driven primarily by their views on the size and duration of AI-related investments," CEO Christophe Fouquet said in a press release. "In light of their demand visibility, some customers are expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030." ASML is the only company in the world that produces extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, a key tool used by the likes of TSMC to make the world's most advanced semiconductors. Investors closely watch the Dutch company's earnings for signs of AI-related chip demand. Fouquet said current supply planned for 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet the demand of its customers. The company is "investigating ways" to increase capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase it had previously forecast. ASML has now updated its guidance three times this year, upping its full-year forecast for the second time in July, and on Wednesday it raised the lower end of its sales forecast for 2026. The company now expects net sales of between 44 billion euros and 45 billion euros ($49.3 billion to $50.4 billion). The previous lower end of the forecast was for 43 billion euros. ASML also said it expects fourth-quarter net sales of between 14.2 billion euros and 15.2 billion euros. The upper end of the range is ahead of LSEG consensus estimates of 14.2 billion euros. ASML's stock was around 2% higher in early trade in Europe. Shares of the company have rallied 56% this year. During the quarter, Samsung and TSMC, the world's two biggest chipmakers, committed to using ASML's High NA extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. High NA EUV is ASML's next-generation tool, which analysts see as key to the Dutch firm's future growth. For the third quarter, here's how ASML did versus LSEG consensus estimates: The semiconductor equipment maker said it expects China sales to account for 20% of its total business, sticking to a prior forecast. While ASML holds an effective monopoly on EUV machines, a July report from The Information suggested an unnamed Chinese company had begun manufacturing an immersion deep ultraviolet lithography (DUV) machine, citing people familiar with the matter. ASML dominates the manufacturing of DUV machines, which are less advanced than EUV. China has been ramping up its domestic semiconductor supply chain, with some investors concerned it could challenge the European and U.S. dominance. However, analysts raised questions about China's ability to ramp up its own DUV technology. ASML meanwhile has faced challenges in China over the last few years. The company is restricted from selling EUV and some DUV tools to China.

title: Anthropic urges court in Washington, DC, to rehear appeal of Pentagon blacklisting
content: Anthropic is asking a federal court in Washington, D.C., to rehear its appeal in a case concerning the Pentagon's blacklisting of the company's AI models. "The Secretary of War branded Anthropic — an American AI company whose models help defend the nation— a national-security 'supply chain risk' because it declined to permit its models to be used for mass surveillance of Americans or lethal autonomous warfare and publicly explained those AI-safety commitments," Anthropic attorneys wrote in the petition filed on Tuesday. "A divided panel upheld that extraordinary designation." The Defense Department, led by Pete Hegseth, applied the supply chain risk label in March, a move that blocked defense contractors from using the company's technology in their work with the agency. That came after a breakdown in negotiations about how the military could use Anthropic's Claude AI models . Anthropic sued the Trump administration in an effort to undo that action. In September, the D.C. Circuit upheld the Pentagon's blacklisting. The 2-1 decision rejected Anthropic's argument that the Department of Defense's ban on its Claude models was arbitrary, unauthorized and unconstitutional. Anthropic's attorneys wrote in the Tuesday filing that the court ignored "straightforward evidence the designation was retaliation for Anthropic's speech about AI safety." In a parallel case, a San Francisco federal judge ruled in August that the DOD had violated Anthropic's First Amendment rights, and that its supply chain risk designation amounted to illegal retaliation. Before the clash between the two sides spilled into the public's view earlier this year, Anthropic served as an early partner across many U.S. agencies, including the DOD. Anthropic signed a $200 million contract with the Pentagon in July of 2025, but as the company began negotiating Claude's deployment on the DOD's GenAI.mil AI platform that September, talks collapsed. A representative from Anthropic declined to comment beyond the filing. A Pentagon spokesperson told CNBC in an email that the agency doesn't comment on pending or ongoing litigation. — CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this report. Fossils of a newly recognized Egyptian crocodile species come from the same rocks as the Great Sphinx, and a missing snout tip helped inspire the animal’s name. Crocodile fossils recovered in Egypt in the 1920s were initially grouped with a living long-snouted crocodile called the false gharial because of their outward resemblance. A new examination, including CT scans that let researchers look inside a nearly complete skull, has identified the Egyptian fossils as a distinct extinct species, Herugavialis cairensis . Dr. Paul Burke, a researcher at the Swedish Museum of Natural History in Stockholm, led the international team from the UK, Sweden, Germany, and Egypt. Advances in paleontological analysis allowed the researchers to identify several differences between the Egyptian fossils and the false gharial, challenging their original assignment to the genus Tomistoma . The fossils came from Egypt’s 45-million-year-old Mokattam Formation. At that time, shallow seas covered much of the region, and Herugavialis shared those waters with at least two other species of gavials, a group of crocodiles distinguished by their long, narrow snouts. Today, gavials live only in freshwater environments on the Indian subcontinent and in Southeast Asia. Just two species survive, Gavialis gangeticus and Tomistoma schlegelii , the false gharial. Their fossil record, however, spans more than 100 million years and documents a nearly worldwide distribution, with many species inhabiting shallow marine environments. The Egyptian skull also has an unusual connection to the Great Sphinx. It comes from the same rocks used to build the monument and, although otherwise relatively well preserved, is missing the tip of its snout. “Given this coincidence with the famously missing nose of the Great Sphinx, we decided to name the new crocodile after the Egyptian god Heru, who was possibly the inspiration for this iconic monument,” says Professor Philip Mannion of University College London, who co-led the study. The shallow seas inhabited by Herugavialis were part of a much longer history of crocodile life across the Mediterranean. “Throughout much of the last 50 million years, the Mediterranean region hosted a high diversity of crocodiles, including gavials,” says Burke, the study’s lead author. “However, this diversity fluctuated over time, seemingly corresponding to changes in global temperature and sea level, before the loss of all crocodiles in this region as a result of the drying of the Mediterranean approximately 6 million years ago.” Reference: “Cranial anatomy of the Middle Eocene Egyptian crocodylian Herugavialis cairensis provides new insights into gavialoid diversity in the Mediterranean region” by Paul M. J. Burke, Stephan N. F. Spiekman, Belal S. Salem, Sara Saber, Hesham M. Sallam and Philip D. Mannion, 1 October 2026, Royal Society Open Science . title: World’s oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
content: Archaeologists working off the coast of Turkey have found a shipwreck dating back around 4,700 years, making it the oldest in the world. A number of ancient storage vessels known as amphorae were recovered during excavations at the wreck, which was found at a depth of around 100 feet near Kekova Island off the coast of southern Turkey, according to a statement from the country’s culture ministry, published Wednesday. The amphorae date from 4,400-4,700 years ago and provide new information on maritime history, the daily lives of mariners and trade connections at the time. The vessels are thought to mainly have been used for transporting olive oil or wine. However, one amphora features a distinctive set of marks and two holes in its body, which suggest it could have been used to make cheese or butter. Researchers said the presence of this amphora may mean that sailors took goats with them on their voyages, using their milk to make dairy products. The excavations were led by Hakan Öniz, a professor at Akdeniz University, Antalya, who told CNN that the shipwreck was first discovered four years ago. The amphorae were initially thought to be much more recent, but then Öniz read a publication on amphorae that had been found near the Giza pyramids in Egypt — the oldest of which was believed to have been under construction at the same time as the ship sank. “These resembled the amphorae in our shipwreck,” Öniz told CNN on Wednesday, adding that a team of researchers made a follow-up dive at the site. They then invited a leading expert on amphorae, Australian archaeologist Karin Sowada, to visit the shipwreck and examine the evidence. “We reached a consensus and proceeded with further analysis,” said Öniz, who added the team are “generally confident” that this is the oldest shipwreck in the world. “It is not just the amphorae; the anchors and other artifacts found at the shipwreck site also point to the same centuries,” he said. Turkey’s culture and tourism minister, Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, said the amphorae appear to have moved around the Eastern Mediterranean. “Clay analyses indicate that the amphorae were likely produced in workshops in the Jordan Valley,” Ersoy said in the statement. “The fact that similar examples have been found in Egypt, Troy, and Crete is of great importance for understanding the trade networks that connected different geographies via sea routes,” he said. Researchers believe the ship may have been traveling from the Levantine coast, which runs from Turkey in the north to Egypt in the south, to Troy or Crete when it was wrecked.

title: Patients' frustration at GP surgery's AI receptionist
content:
Patients have described their "frustration" in dealing with a new AI receptionist tool at their GP surgery, which some said was a "wall" to receiving care.
Newbury Street Practice, in Wantage, Oxfordshire, began using the AI Andi triage system in July, with all calls made to the surgery passing through the bot.
A spokesperson for the surgery said majority of feedback regarding the new system had been positive, and that it would "improve access" and "increase capacity".
But patient Jo Rogers is one of those who have criticised the system and said the AI bot "puts you off ever bothering" contacting the practice.
"I had to get through AI Andy's 'wall' recently," Rogers said.
She said she had been waiting in a phone queue for 20 minutes, after which "he decided he couldn't help me".
All calls to the surgery go through the AI system, which can then pass them onto a human receptionist, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
In an introduction post about the system, the practice website said Andi "listens carefully, understands how you're feeling, and helps you get what you need quickly".
But some patients have raised their concerns. Among them is 65-year-old Tricia Lockhart, who said she was left "frustrated" after the AI system thought she was "calling about pregnancy".
"Quite an achievement for a 65-year-old," she said.
A spokesperson for the surgery said the purpose of introducing the technology was "to improve access, increase capacity and allow staff to spend more time supporting patients who are unable or choose not to use our digital options".
But user John Allinson disagreed, saying: "AI is all about cutting costs and saving money." The GP practice disputes this claim.
Local MP Olly Glover recently contributed to the debate, after being contacted by residents in his Didcot and Wantage constituency.
He said he had been in touch with the GP surgery who "like many other surgeries, are trying to streamline their administrative processes".
"There is clearly pressure on primary care services across our constituency, where we have seen high levels of housing growth," he said.
"Successive governments have not taken the need to provide health and other infrastructure ahead of new homes seriously enough."
In the first month of its installation, a spokesperson for Newbury Street Surgery said feedback on the AI tool had been "79% positive".
"We know some patients, particularly those less confident with technology, have found the change harder, and as with any new system it takes time to settle," they said.
"We continue to review our processes, systems and feedback regularly post implementation to shape next steps including any future support our patients may require. "

title: The genetic technique that finds (almost) every infection
content:
It identified Covid-19. Now this genetic technique is helping doctors to make life-or-death decisions.
In late December 2019, a team of virologists from three major Chinese cities began analysing swabs taken from patients hospitalised with mysterious cases of severe pneumonia.
All had been present at the Huanan Seafood Market, Wuhan, before rapidly falling unwell. But when the virologists ran the samples, they drew a blank: the genetic material did not match any previously discovered pathogen.
The doctors turned to a new screening method known as metagenomic testing. Instead of checking for known microbes, the test could reveal all the microorganisms present in the samples – previously identified or not.
It enabled them to see that the pathogen in the patients' samples bore a close resemblance to the coronavirus family, a group that included viruses which had previously caused outbreaks of severe pneumonia in humans, such as Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (Mers). The scientists had just discovered Covid-19.
"It was a gamechanger compared with previous pandemics," says Niranjan Nagarajan, an associate professor at the National University of Singapore. Knowing what the pathogen was made it possible to rapidly develop Covid diagnostics to try to curb the spread, and kickstarted the frantic search for treatments and vaccines around the globe .
This remains the best-known use of metagenomics to date. But the test is now increasingly being used in hospitals. And from quickly diagnosing sepsis to identifying the causes of unexplained ailments, it's already saving lives.
Whenever a patient arrives in a neurological ward displaying signs of confusion and drowsiness, and complaining of fever, headache and weakness, doctors are acutely aware that it could be a life-or-death emergency.
How metagenomic testing works
Metagenomics, the study of all the DNA and RNA found in a particular environment, is seen as an increasingly important clinical approach . Metagenomic testing involves extracting genetic material from a sample, then using advanced sequencing methods to identify the genetic codes of everything that's there. These results can be analysed by computers with reference to large databases, allowing doctors to pinpoint the exact organisms present, such as bacteria or viruses.
This constellation of symptoms can indicate meningitis or encephalitis – deadly conditions affecting the brain and spinal cord. Yet doctors often face a critical dilemma. The most suitable treatment would depend on whether the patient's condition was due to a virus or bacteria, or an overreaction from the brain's immune system. With limited tests and time, however, doctors are often forced to hedge their bets.
"You need to make a decision immediately," says Charles Chiu, a professor and infectious diseases expert at the University of California San Francisco Department of Medicine in the US, who has been carrying out new studies into the use of metagenomic tests. "Currently, with patients who are critically ill, doctors treat them for infection and for autoimmune disease."
In some ways, this is contradictory, because it involves suppressing the patient's immune system even though they might have an infection. "But there's often no other choice," says Chiu.
Metagenomics is now helping to inform these decisions. Chiu and his colleagues have developed a pioneering metagenomics test for identifying pathogens within cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid that bathes the brain and spinal cord. The test has already flagged cases where, unbeknownst to doctors, a pathogen was driving a patient's symptoms.
For example, Chiu encountered a patient who had been diagnosed with meningitis and liver failure, and was scheduled to receive a liver transplant. But the metagenomics test on her spinal fluid revealed that she was actually infected with the hepatitis E virus. While hepatitis E is a known and treatable cause of liver disease, it is not commonly tested for in high-income countries such as the US.
"We gave her an antiviral medication, she got better, and we spared her from undergoing the transplant," says Chiu.
Until recently, the use of metagenomics has been limited by the length of time required for the analysis. Separating human and microbial DNA, and identifying the signs of a potentially worrisome pathogen, requires highly specialist skills. "Doing the sequencing and the analysis can take several days to a week," says Nagarajan. "The patient might die before you're able to get a result."
Now, though, machines can sequence DNA within as little as one to two hours, and AI tools can ingest vast datasets to decipher patterns within them. And it's finally making metagenomics more widely accessible.
For people with poorly functioning immune systems, any infection can swiftly turn into a potentially deadly threat. Transplant recipients, cancer patients undergoing immune-suppressing treatment and those living with autoimmune diseases must be on constant high alert.
Studies have suggested that immunosuppressed patients who develop sepsis or blood poisoning due to an infection are at a 23% higher risk of dying in hospital. However, making a quick diagnosis in these cases is not always easy.

title: Broadband fears after fibre works stop in village
content:
Residents in a rural Kent village have raised concerns they could be left without broadband access after fibre installation works stopped.
Work began in August in Hunton to replace existing copper broadband infrastructure with fibre cables, but residents said it stopped after a few days.
Some residents said they had been told they might need to find another broadband provider, but they did not know what was happening.
Kings Hill-based firm Trooli said it had not been possible to extend its fibre network and affected customers had been contacted. Openreach said the old network would close on 31 January 2027 and customers would need to move to a digital phone service by then.
Resident Rodney Ballard told the Local Democracy Reporting Service that Trooli had given notice to some residents that their connections would be terminated, while Openreach had said copper connections would be withdrawn.
"There's no real plan being told to residents how this is going to happen," he said.
Hunton parish and Maidstone borough councillor Mike Summersgill said residents had welcomed the start of installation work but then "all of a sudden the road closure and barriers were taken away".
After work stopped, he said: "My worry is for the single, elderly constituents who rely purely on the landline to keep in touch with family or to be talked to by doctors."
Leah Istratescu, from Staplehurst, who works at Hunton and Linton Pre-School, said reliable broadband was essential for running the school and communicating with parents, adding: "It's really important that we keep them updated."
A Trooli spokesperson said the broadband service had been delivered using Openreach copper infrastructure that was being withdrawn.
The company said it had explored extending its fibre network, but said: "Unfortunately, there are few locations where, because of excessive costs, we have had to conclude this is simply not possible."
Trooli said it had contacted affected customers and advised them of other broadband options.
After some customers said they had been told the copper broadband switch-off would be on 23 October, an Openreach spokesperson said: "Openreach has no plans to switch off services supporting broadband or phone lines in the village this October."
They said: "Decisions about Trooli's services or its fibre rollout in Hunton are for the company and are separate from the closure of the analogue phone network.
"Anyone concerned about their service should speak to their communications provider - the company they pay their bill to - about the options available."
The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport said rural communities should not be left behind in the rollout of faster broadband.
It said: "We are investing billions of pounds to bring internet upgrades to hard-to-reach homes and businesses that would otherwise miss out - including in Kent.
"Where commercial rollout plans change, the government will work with suppliers to explore alternative ways to connect affected communities."
